section_title: Why did relief from the frogs not lead Pharaoh to keep his word?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 1 Then the LORD said to Moses, “Go to Pharaoh and tell him that this is what the LORD says: ‘Let My people go, so that they may worship Me. 2 But if you refuse to let them go, I will plague your whole country with frogs. 3 The Nile will teem with frogs, and they will come into your palace and up to your bedroom and onto your bed, into the houses of your officials and your people, and into your ovens and kneading bowls. 4 The frogs will come up on you and your people and all your officials.’” 5 And the LORD said to Moses, “Tell Aaron, ‘Stretch out your hand with your staff over the rivers and canals and ponds, and cause the frogs to come up onto the land of Egypt.’” 6 So Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt, and the frogs came up and covered the land of Egypt. 7 But the magicians did the same thing by their magic arts, and they also brought frogs up onto the land of Egypt.

8 Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said, “Pray to the LORD to take the frogs away from me and my people. Then I will let your people go, that they may sacrifice to the LORD.” 9 Moses said to Pharaoh, “You may have the honor over me. When shall I pray for you and your officials and your people that the frogs (except for those in the Nile) may be taken away from you and your houses?” 10 “Tomorrow,” Pharaoh answered. “May it be as you say,” Moses replied, “so that you may know that there is no one like the LORD our God. 11 The frogs will depart from you and your houses and your officials and your people; they will remain only in the Nile.”

12 After Moses and Aaron had left Pharaoh, Moses cried out to the LORD for help with the frogs that He had brought against Pharaoh. 13 And the LORD did as Moses requested, and the frogs in the houses, the courtyards, and the fields died. 14 They were piled into countless heaps, and there was a terrible stench in the land. 15 When Pharaoh saw that there was relief, however, he hardened his heart and would not listen to Moses and Aaron, just as the LORD had said.

context_lines: God again commands Pharaoh to release His people for worship, this time warning of frogs throughout the country. They enter bedrooms, beds, ovens and kneading bowls. The plague carries the disturbance into the most ordinary parts of home life. The magicians bring up more frogs, adding to what is already overwhelming the land.

Frogs also had a place in Egyptian religion. The [Global Egyptian Museum](https://www.globalegyptianmuseum.org/glossary.aspx?id=180) describes Heqet as a goddess shown as a frog or with a frog’s head, associated with life and childbirth. That supplies cultural background for the reversal here: creatures associated with new life have become an unbearable intrusion.

Pharaoh now asks Moses and Aaron to pray to the LORD and promises to release the people. Moses lets him choose when the frogs should be removed, so he may know there is no one like the LORD. Pharaoh chooses the next day.

Moses prays, God answers, and the frogs outside the Nile die. Their heaps leave a terrible smell, but the immediate pressure has eased. Pharaoh responds to that relief by hardening his heart and refusing to listen. His promise does not survive the end of the crisis.
common_interpretation_lines: The shared reading distinguishes asking for relief from a lasting willingness to obey. [Calvin](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/exodus/8.htm) and [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-second-book-of-moses-called-exodus/) both emphasize Pharaoh returning to resistance after the pressure is removed, while God’s answer to Moses demonstrates His authority over the plague.
god_plan_lines: Moses prays for the ruler who is resisting God, and God removes the plague. This is an example of praying on someone else’s behalf. [1 Timothy 2:1–6](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_timothy/2.htm) later calls believers to pray for everyone, including rulers, and names Christ Jesus as the One who brings people to God and gave Himself as a ransom.

There is also a wider parallel with Christ’s work for His people. [Hebrews 7:23–27](https://biblehub.com/bsb/hebrews/7.htm) describes Jesus as the enduring high priest who always lives to intercede for those who come to God through Him. Moses’ prayer brings temporary relief from a plague; Jesus’ priestly work brings complete salvation. The parallel points toward the fuller help found in Christ.
